item.title: [BBC World] Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Gadi Eisenkot has vowed to oust Benjamin Netanyahu, but still has to get enough parties on boardByRaffi BergPublished10 November 2026, 12:25 GMTUpdated 21 minutes ago
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.
Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.
"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.
He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".
Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.
"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."

European Union nations have not made any commitments on bolstering security in the Red Sea, Italy's defense minister said Tuesday.
"I have yet to see anything concrete," Guido Crosetto told the Reuters news agency.
Crosetto in September called on the EU to boost security as part of its Aspides mission, the aim of which is to protect commercial shipping from coming under fire by Iran or its Yemeni allies, the Houthi rebels, in the Red Sea and surrounding waters.
The Houthis intensified attacks in the Red Sea, targeting Saudi-linked vessels over the summer, in response to Saudi Arabia's backing of Yemeni government forces in the country's decade-long civil war.

French police have made arrests after three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, were searched in relation to an investigation into Mohamed Al Fayed's abuse.
The Paris prosecutor's office told the BBC that several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released.
In a confidential letter sent to survivors, the Metropolitan Police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in what is understood to be a joint operation between British and French authorities.

The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed.
The late Egyptian billionaire bought the Ritz Paris hotel in 1979, and it is still owned by the Al Fayed family.
The Villa Windsor in western Paris, another property involved in the search, was a holiday home for the Al Fayed family. It was previously the home of King Edward VIII, following his abdication, and his wife Wallis Simpson.

item.title: [Guardian China] ‘Flying cars’ could launch in China next summer, maker of two-seat model says
item.description:
Aridge unveils new modular 'flying car'
‘Flying cars’ could launch in China next summer, maker of two-seat model says
XPeng says its $300k low-altitude device will soon be ready for emergency services and recreational use in rural areas
People could start taking trips in so-called flying cars in China as soon as next summer, the manufacturer of a two-seater vehicle with autopilot model has said.
Deli Zhao, the chief executive of the Chinese flying car company XPeng, said the $300,000 (£225,000) low-altitude device would be ready for use by recreational users in rural locations and by emergency services in the second half of 2027. After 10 years of development including trials of flying motorbikes at the company’s Guangzhou base, it has been approved by China’s civil aviation authorities for limited use.
The small cockpit is about the size of a Fiat 500 car and the vehicle is lifted into the air by six drone-like battery-powered propellers and steered by a simple joystick. It can also fly autonomously to a programmed destination, but Xhao, a trained pilot, claimed he could teach anyone to fly it in five minutes.
The price tag for the contraption includes a six-wheel van about the size of a Ford Transit, out of the back of which the flying vehicle unfolds “just like the Transformers”, said Zhao. He has been developing flying cars for almost a decade and said he was part-inspired by the flying creatures ridden by humans in the Harry Potter stories and the Green Goblin’s flying skateboard from the Spider-Man comics.
View image in fullscreen
The flying car during a demonstration in Dubai last month. Photograph: Giuseppe Cacace/AFP/Getty Images
“The world where everyone can be a captain is about to arrive,” he said at the Web Summit in Lisbon on Tuesday, where a prototype of the vehicle drew large crowds. item.title: [CBS News World] France says Iran behind costly grocery store refrigeration hacks
item.description:
French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, the Paris prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks. On Tuesday, France's foreign minister said the country "rules nothing out" in its response to what he called "a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country."
The Oct. 11 hacking attack struck major supermarket chains, hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.
The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by similar hacks affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. A separate cyberattack targeted several blood banks in France, but the products and samples were not damaged.
In August, refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases sparked an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News. Hamilton told CBS News this week that the division's Cyber Field Office was working with French law enforcement to understand the refrigeration outages in Europe.
There has been no assertion yet by officials in France, the U.S. or the other European nations hit by the hacks that all of the incidents were connected.
In its statement Monday, the Paris public prosecutor's office said its cybercrime division had opened a judicial investigation on charges including "fraudulent interference with an automated data-processing system and causing damage by means dangerous to persons — both committed as part of an organized group."

item.description:
The U.S. military moved nine Stratotanker refueling planes from a base in England to facilities in Germany and Spain on Monday, and The Wall Street Journal quoted sources as saying they had been repositioned due to a threat from Iran.
It is unclear whether the threat was imminent or general, the sources told the newspaper.
A U.S. official told CBS News later Tuesday that there were credible threats against bases in the U.K., without specifying who was behind the threats.
CBS News Confirmed found public aircraft tracking data showing 10 KC-135 Stratotankers were moved from Royal Air Force Base Mildenhall, in southeast England to other locations. One landed at Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland, while four went to Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany and one landed at Ramstein Air Base, the headquarters of the U.S. Forces Europe, also in Germany.
Four more Stratotankers left Mildenhall and arrived Monday at Morón Air Base in southern Spain.

Ben Birchall/Getty
"We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure," a U.S. official told CBS News on Tuesday, without commenting on specific aircraft movements.
Three U.S. Osprey tiltrotor transport planes also departed RAF Mildenhall and arrived Tuesday at RAF Lakenheath, another base used by the U.S. in England. It is unclear whether all of the movements were linked to the reported threat from Iran.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

item.title: [BBC World] First day of Ukraine peace talks 'very productive', US says
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Senior officials from Ukraine, Russia and the US will reconvene on Wednesday for a second day of talksByLaura Gozzi and Abdujalil Abdurasulov, Reporting fromKyivPublished10 November 2026, 00:09 GMTUpdated 2 hours ago
The first day of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi.
While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions - due to resume on Wednesday - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who did not attend the talks, said they had been "very productive".
Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.
At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".
Kushner said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
He and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting.
European leaders have largely been excluded from peace talks until now, but they have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them.
The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".
However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.

US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry
Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’
Cop31 live – latest updates
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. item.title: [Guardian China] Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller
item.description:
No more getting away with it … Traces of Justice. Photograph: Trinity/CineAsia
View image in fullscreen
No more getting away with it … Traces of Justice. Photograph: Trinity/CineAsiaReview
Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller
Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases
The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise, offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative. It’s essentially a portmanteau biopic: its hero is Cui Xun, a fictional stand-in for the venerable Cui Daozhi, a still-extant real-life figure who so revolutionised forensic science he became known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. Ripping three-and-a-bit tales from the casebook – involving a 1970s child killer, a grisly 1980s multiple murder and a 1990s bus bombing (plus one lingering loose end), Chen constructs a history of forensic investigation that is also, in variably oblique ways, a history of Chinese law enforcement, which is shown evolving from boozy, gloveless crime-scene trampling to something far more streamlined and professional.
Within the handsome period framework, Chen follows the science: one era’s crazy innovation becomes commonplace in the next. A rookie Cui (played here by Zhang Yi, ageing up subtly) uses boiled potatoes to take dental imprints; when these run out, he and his colleagues start biting one another’s cheeks to make their points. (Their scars are a terrific visual gag: scientists literally showing their working.) By the 90s, when Cui is heading a team working out of a vast, well-staffed warehouse, we seem mere moments away from David Caruso’s sunglasses and memorable Who guitar riffs. item.description:
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByArchie MitchellBusiness reporterPublished9 November 2026
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

Death toll rises to 39 after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal
The death toll in Senegal’s boat capsize has risen to 39 after new bodies were discovered Monday, according to the country’s emergency servicesByBABAKAR DIONE Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 6:40 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
DAKAR, Senegal -- The death toll from the capsize off Senegal of a boat carrying migrants rose to 39 following the discovery of more bodies on Monday, the country’s emergency services said.
The boat, which left Saint-Louis in northern Senegal and was headed to the Spanish coast, overturned on Sunday, offshore from the town of Kébémer, north of the capital Dakar.
The Ministry of Interior said Sunday at least 21 people had died and rescuers were looking for possible survivors. It did not say how many people were on the boat, but several passengers are still believed to be missing.
Only one passenger was rescued alive.

item.title: [ABC News World] He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon's presidential bid may hand it power
item.description:
He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon's presidential bid may hand it power
Jean-Luc Mélenchon is 75 and he's betting his last shot at France’s presidency on a generation young enough to be his grandchildrenByTHOMAS ADAMSON Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 12:03 AM
Share
LE BOURGET, France -- Young supporters wore his name on their backs like a soccer star’s, above the number 27. They sang about brass bands and revolution. Many had spent the fall protesting or blockading their schools.
Then in walked Jean-Luc Mélenchon: 75 years old, on his fourth presidential run and old enough to be their grandfather.
“I have only one sensible thing to propose,” he told 20,000 supporters in a vast hall north of Paris on Saturday. “Everything must change.”
The septuagenarian may never get another chance. Three presidential bids have ended short of the runoff. In 2022, just 421,308 votes kept him out. Now, riding a surge in support, he is eyeing a winner-take-all showdown with far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen.
The bespectacled, booming and seemingly tireless leftist wants more than the presidency. He wants to rewrite the rules of the French republic — invoking the unfinished promise of the Revolution of 1789.
A place in the May 2 runoff could prove a cruel prize. If Le Pen beats him, the anti-capitalist who has spent half a century fighting the far right could help give it what it has never won: the Elysee Palace — and command of France’s nuclear arsenal.
Victory could send shock waves across the Atlantic. Trump would still be in the White House. Russia is waging war in Ukraine. Yet Mélenchon wants to pull the EU’s only nuclear-armed power out of NATO, starting with its military command. His debt plans could also put France on a collision course with Europe’s central bank, rattling markets.

View image in fullscreen
People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.
An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.
The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.
Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.
Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.
Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.
View image in fullscreen
People search for survivors after the collision. Photograph: AP
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

View image in fullscreen
Daniel Oyegade on the shoot for Homage, a See My World production. Photograph: Omar Balaa
How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
